body: Brazilian licence plates changed in 2018 to white with a blue stripe on top, while red plates remain for commercial vehicles.
Portuguese is spoken in Brazil, unlike most Latin American countries that speak Spanish; it differs notably with suffixes -ão, and sounds like -ch and -nh.
Soil in Brazil is mostly red, varying from light pink in Mato Grosso to deep maroon near the Paraná river, but usually not red in the Northeast or most of Rio Grande do Sul.
Common Brazilian poles resemble a ladder at the bottom with rectangular shape, long segments, and small holes near the top.
Most Brazilian road signs have black-painted backs.
Blue road markers with road numbers and kilometres are commonly seen alongside Brazilian roads.
Brazil uses yellow on black chevrons for road markers, unlike most South American countries that use black on yellow.
Brazilian roads usually have double yellow middle lines flanked by white outer lines, sometimes with a single dashed yellow line.
White painted curbs are frequently found along Brazilian roads.
Many Brazilian houses feature orange tiled roofs.
Transparent satellite dishes are fairly common in Brazil, making them generally unique in Latin America.
Blue Fortlev water tanks are often visible on roofs throughout Brazil.
Generation 3 coverage cars in Brazil include white cars with stubby antennas wrapped in diagonal coils or without antennas, similar to cars in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico.
Generation 4 cars found in Brazil have visible fronts with colors: blue, white with a blue stripe, or plain white.
Brazil features Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, mounted lower with a large circular blur and small front protrusion; only Brazil and Peru have this in South America.
Brazil's coverage is mostly in the eastern half, with sparse Amazon coverage; early players should note limited western coverage to avoid plonking far from roads.
Area codes in Brazil are common, usually in parentheses or as two numbers; codes ending in 1 correspond to major cities and capitals.
Brazilian states have two-letter acronyms, notably used on state road markers, aiding quick geographic identification.
Brazilian postcodes (CEP) appear frequently on street signs and start in São Paulo, progressing anti-clockwise to Rio Grande do Sul.
Brazil's elevation map shows highest mountains near the southeastern coast and flatter regions elsewhere.
Northeastern Brazil's Caatinga landscape is marked by dry soil, shrubs, and succulents, which remain discernible even in the rainy season.
The Amazon rainforest covers 40% of Brazil, with few roads passing through dense forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.
Acre features small grassy hills with sparse trees; roads often go over hills rather than around them, similar to some areas near Maraba in Pará.
Roraima's rural areas consist mainly of open grassy plains with distant mountains; grass grows thinly in bunches.
Rio Grande do Sul features hilly or flat terrain with lush green fields, with southern parts resembling Uruguay.
Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, and Espírito Santo are often characterized by rolling grassy hills.
Espírito Santo and nearby areas have large mountains with exposed rock formations.
Paraná pines have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the ends and grow mainly in the southern states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
Coconut palms grow tall with thin trunks and long leaves, common in northeastern Brazil and along parts of the coast, but are not unique to Brazil.
Carnaúba palms have short fan-like leaves and a smooth spiked trunk, common mainly in Ceará, Piauí, and Rio Grande do Norte.
Babassu palms have long robust leaves with many leaflets, varying trunk lengths, and are found throughout the Amazon and occasionally along the east coast.
Açaí palms produce globally popular fruits, are mostly near Belém, and are identified by drooping leaflets and unusually thin trunks.
Moriche palms have rounded fan-shaped leaves, common in Amazonas, Acre, Roraima, and all Amazonian states; they are also found in Amazon regions of Colombia and Peru.
Macaw palms feature thin leaves and spear-shaped tops, common near Mato Grosso do Sul; caution advised when using single trees as indicators.
Plants with long stems and many leaves are common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba; long stems remain visible in the dry season without leaves.
Very tall grass is often seen in central Brazil, especially in Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais.
Eucalyptus Grandis are very tall trees planted widely across Brazil, common in the south and some large plantations in Amapá.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in São Paulo and coastal northeastern states like Alagoas and Pernambuco.
Soybeans are leafy plants mainly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.
Coffee beans are predominantly grown in Minas Gerais, with presence in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.
Round poles made of concrete are common in southern Brazil, especially São Paulo; city centers usually feature round poles regardless of state.
Wooden poles are mostly used in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
Electricity pole supports connecting crossbar to the stem vary by state and are rare in the northeast; applicable only to poles with crossbars.
Yellow pole ID paint with black codes identifies poles, with those starting with letters seen in Bahia and Pernambuco.
Goiás poles use long yellow paint with black codes starting with numbers, plus a rarer yellow on black ID in paint or plate form.
Small yellow/orange plates attached by metal or zip tie act as pole IDs in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco, positioned higher in Pernambuco.
Paraná pole IDs usually feature black paint with yellow or white painted text.
Most Maranhão poles have small beige plates with built-in numbers; rarely this ID appears in Pará and Piauí.
Utility poles in Paraná intersections sometimes display street names; this occasionally occurs in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
São Paulo's common poletop has an asymmetrical crossbar with a central support, also seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, and Mato Grosso do Sul.
Asymmetrical crossbars without supports are exclusive to Ceará and Rondônia, with Ceará using concrete and Rondônia metal crossbars.
Zigzag-shaped top bars on poles are unique to Ceará and Roraima and are generally much larger than regular poles.
'Pencil poles' with smooth cone tops are common in Rio de Janeiro and rare in Brasília and Manaus.
Gamma-shaped poles with electricity boxes are common in Rio de Janeiro and some northern cities; a shorter bar variant exists only in Belém.
Electricity counters attached to poles are frequently seen in Cuiabá, Macapá, and major cities in Pará; counters may have one or multiple compartments.
Poles with one top insulator and horizontal alternating insulators are found in Mato Grosso, southern Acre, and rarely in Rio Grande do Sul.
Brown mushroom-shaped insulators are exclusive to Pernambuco.
White mushroom-shaped insulators are found in Bahia and occasionally in Brasília.
Transparent insulators are common in Alagoas and Santa Catarina, and rarely seen in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.
Thread spool-shaped insulators mostly appear in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been reported in Ceará.
Uniquely long and thin insulators occur in Ceará and rarely in Goiás.
Poles with horizontal insulators are common in Pará, less so in Mato Grosso, and rare in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
Long grey insulators (non-horizontal) primarily appear in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná, and Santa Catarina; rarely in some other states.
Black double UFO-shaped insulators in trident formation are common in Maranhão, though the insulator itself is widespread in different forms.
'Lollipop' insulators are spherical or cone-shaped, suspended above the insulator bar, common in Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and rarely Sergipe.
Dark brown insulators with grey bases are almost exclusive to Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Trash baskets in Brazil are mostly metal, but in Acre and Rondônia, concrete bins are more common outside houses.
Lamps in Minas Gerais and Goiás often have two parts and also appear in Rio Grande do Norte, Ceará, Rio Grande do Sul, and the Federal District.
Urban northern Paraná lamps sometimes lack lamp arms and vary between colorful industrial or ornate styles, mostly in northwest Paraná.
In several states, lamps usually have arms attached directly to the poles, unlike the more common plate attachments elsewhere.
Roraima lamps share styles but vary in colors depending on the city.
Ceará lamps often have fancy colorful arms and sometimes display the town name.
São Paulo has the most divided highways among Brazilian states.
Phone numbers can sometimes be found under São Paulo's kilometer markers.
Cobblestone pavements are most common in Brazil's northeast and Rio Grande do Sul.
Hexagonal concrete tile roads appear across Brazil but are more frequent in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
Some Acre roads are made of red bricks.
Randomly sized cobblestone roads are common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.
Uneven square stone roads appear in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina; soil here is often very dark.
Brown-tiled pavements in Rio Grande do Sul are jagged, random, or square and sometimes seen in Santa Catarina.
Southern Brazilian buildings (mainly Santa Catarina) show European, often German, architectural influence.
Wooden houses on stilts are common in Acre and occasionally in Amazonas and Pará.
Piauí roads mostly have red gravel shoulders; some newer roads have tarmac with curbs.
Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features a smudged front-right camera and a white car with a blue stripe.
Generation 3 coverage in Alagoas often shows rifts.
João-de-Barro nests are spherical structures atop utility poles, common in southern Brazil.
Uiramuta, northern Roraima has a dry landscape with large mountains featuring numerous folds.
Coastal Rio Grande do Sul is notable for rare flat wetlands uncommon in Brazil.
São Paulo's pole ID paint is square and yellow, featuring a three-letter municipality code, two numbers, a black line, and four more numbers.
Street signs in Campo Grande and Joinville are stickers wrapped around poles, with Campo Grande signs often having extra info and a red-yellow stripe.
Rio de Janeiro lamps have uniquely curved lamp arms not seen elsewhere.
Teresina lamps are typically blue with orange arms.
Belém lamp heads are often orange.
Cuiabá lamps are light green and feature poles with multiple electricity meters (sometimes 6 to 12).
Belo Horizonte and Uberaba lamps in Generation 4 sometimes have white, numbered plaques; this feature may expand to other Minas Gerais cities.
Caxias do Sul lamps often have zigzag bent poles with yellow heads.
Santa Catarina Island poles (Florianópolis) are painted white with blue and red stripes.
Northwest Rio Grande do Sul has Generation 3 coverage affected by a camera glitch.
Acre's road 364 has a unique 'rollercoaster' landscape where the road rides hills instead of winding; mostly covered by Generation 3 with antenna and low traffic.
Amazonas 319 road cuts through lush tropical rainforest with mostly unpaved roads and orange soil, paved near Manaus, lined with wooden or ladder poles, covered by blue Generation 4 car.
Pará section of road 163 is hilly, curvy, dry, hazy with diverse Amazon vegetation; heavily trafficked by trucks and covered by blue Generation 4 car.
Amazonian trekkers combine boat and walking coverage near Madeira and Aripuana rivers through rainforest and small villages.
National Park in Northeast Maranhão has walking, trekker, and vehicle coverage across sand dunes and pools, with landscapes varying from beach to sandy wetlands.

Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is a Brazilian island northeast of Rio Grande do Norte with official coverage, similar vegetation to nearby mainland, large exposed rocks, white buggy coverage, and boat coverage around the island.
